rv.q: If you’re looking for an entirely satisfying night of oldfangled entertainment, you might consider being there, too.

Daniel Radcliffe makes a charming Broadway debut in this slick revival of the Frank Loesser musical, bringing boyish enthusiasm and surprising song-and-dance skills to the role of ambitious window washer J. Pierrepont Finch.
That production made the piece look weary and faded; in director Rob Ashford’s hands, “How to Succeed” springs back to life.
After “Equus,” Radcliffe aims to establish himself as a quadruple threat: He acts, sings, dances and delivers a perfectly fine American accent.
Rob Ashford has lit the lights with a smart and satisfying production of 'How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying.'
Daniel Radcliffe brings boyish charm and surprising comic timing to the role of J. Pierrepont Finch
Somehow it doesn't matter. He works so hard that we're on his side even if he, like his character, doesn't have the creds.
He sings. He dances. Yes, the British mega-star formerly known as young Harry Potter even shaves, proudly, while delivering that irresistibly all-American self-love ballad.
The musical numbers too rarely catch fire, despite the hard-sell athleticism of his choreography.
Mr. Radcliffe the only reason to see the show, and contrary to what the title suggests, this young actor really, really tries.
“Bengal Tiger,” which was nominated for a Pulitzer Prize, may work on the page, but it is numbing and listless on the stage.
If it doesn't measure up in terms of evergreens the score is sharp and witty, and the satire of Madison Avenue values stands up surprisingly well, 60-odd years on.
Radcliffe gets an A for effort, but he doesn’t have the theatrical stature to pull together this choppy production
His concept for the early '60s satire of American business is to stylistically turn up the volume, saturating the stage in candy colors and frantic dances.
In fact, Radcliffe ultimately succeeds not by overshadowing his fellow cast members, but by working in conscientious harmony with them — and having a blast in the process.
In fact, the show itself - arguably the peppiest, cheeriest, most charming Broadway revival since The Pajama Game five seasons back - never seems dated
Naked ambition has seldom been so appealing.
Seeing young Daniel Radcliffe's poised and skillful performance in this very challenging role, I'm wondering if the famed movie actor may have found his true calling.
In that department, if not in all others, he most certainly overachieved.
Even though the musical depicts a dated, sexist work culture similar to the one found on TV's "Mad Men," it remains absolutely timeless and hilarious.
His current transformation into a song-and-dance man isn’t quite so convincing in “How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying.”
As for the appealing Radcliffe, he’s eager to please but lacks a certain urgency that makes Finch dangerous and irresistible at the same time.
And much of How to Succeeds satire, like much of its pure fun, remains surprisingly fresh.
While this production directed and choreographed by Rob Ashford rarely hits the musical comedy heights that it should, it’s a solidly entertaining rendition that should well please audiences.
The featured players are good but their performances appear to be dialed down somewhat in deference to their star.
Individually, the entire cast is quite strong, but what they collectively lack is chemistry.
